specStatements.text: Everyday electrical appliances are designed to bring about energy transfers.
The amount of energy an appliance transfers depends on how long the appliance is switched on for and the power of the appliance.
Students should be able to describe how different domestic appliances transfer energy from batteries or ac mains to the kinetic energy of electric motors or the energy of heating devices.
Work is done when charge flows in a circuit.
The amount of energy transferred by electrical work can be calculated using the equation:
energy transferred = power × time
[E = P t]
energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference
[E = Q V]
energy transferred, E, in joules, J
power, P, in watts, W
time, t, in seconds, s
charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C
potential difference, V, in volts, V
Students should be able to explain how the power of a circuit device is related to:
• the potential difference across it and the current through it
• the energy transferred over a given time.
Students should be able to describe, with examples, the relationship between the power ratings for domestic electrical appliances and the changes in stored energy when they are in use.
The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
Electrical power is transferred from power stations to consumers using the National Grid.

Step-up transformers are used to increase the potential difference from the power station to the transmission cables then step-down transformers are used to decrease, to a much lower value, the potential difference for domestic use.
Students should be able to explain why the National Grid system is an efficient way to transfer energy.

concepts.definition: An everyday electrical appliance such as a kettle, a lamp or a food mixer is designed to bring about a particular energy transfer when a current flows through it.
The amount of energy an appliance transfers depends on two things: how long the appliance is switched on for, and the power of the appliance.
In appliances such as a food mixer, a drill or a washing machine, energy is transferred electrically from batteries or the ac mains to the kinetic energy of an electric motor.
In appliances such as a kettle, a toaster or an iron, energy is transferred electrically from the ac mains to a heating device, raising the temperature of water, food or metal.
Portable appliances are usually supplied by batteries, which provide a direct current. Appliances plugged into sockets are supplied by the ac mains.
Work is done when charge flows in a circuit. The energy transferred by that work comes from the store associated with the source, such as the chemical store of a battery.
The energy transferred by electrical work can be calculated from the power of the device and the time for which it operates: energy transferred = power x time.
The symbol form of energy transferred = power x time, where E is energy transferred in joules, P is power in watts and t is time in seconds.

concepts.term: energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference
concepts.definition: The energy transferred by electrical work can also be calculated from the charge that flows and the potential difference it moves through: energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference.
The symbol form of energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference, where E is energy transferred in joules, Q is charge flow in coulombs and V is potential difference in volts.
Energy transferred, E, is measured in joules, J. One joule is transferred when a power of one watt operates for one second.
Time, t, is measured in seconds, s, in E = P t. Times given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before the equation is used.
Charge flow, Q, is measured in coulombs, C. A charge flow of one coulomb passes when a current of one ampere flows for one second.

concepts.term: Energy transferred over a given time
concepts.definition: Because energy transferred = power x time, the power of a device is the energy it transfers divided by the time in seconds. Two devices can transfer the same energy at different powers if they run for different times.

The power rating printed on an appliance is the power it transfers when working normally. A higher power rating means a faster change in the stored energy of the appliance and its surroundings while it is in use.
The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers that links power stations to consumers such as homes, schools and factories.
A step-up transformer increases the potential difference from the power station to the transmission cables, which reduces the current in those cables for the same power.
A step-down transformer decreases the potential difference, to a much lower value, for domestic use, so that mains electricity reaches consumers at a safe potential difference.
Transmitting at a high potential difference means a low current in the cables. Because the power wasted by heating the cables is given by P = I^2 R, a lower current wastes much less energy.

misconceptions.question: A kettle is labelled 2000 W. How much energy does it transfer?
misconceptions.correct: The label gives the power, not the energy. Energy transferred also depends on time: E = P t, so 2000 W for 90 s transfers 180 000 J.
misconceptions.misconception: The number on the label is the energy, so a 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Power and energy are both 'how much' quantities in everyday speech, and the rating is the only number printed on the appliance.
misconceptions.correction: Read the watt as 'joules every second'. Multiply the power by the number of seconds to get the energy transferred.

misconceptions.question: A 12 V supply drives a current of 0.25 A through a device. What is the power?
misconceptions.misconception: In an electrical power or energy equation I am unsure whether to multiply or divide the two quantities, so I use the wrong operation - e.g. dividing pd by current to find power, or multiplying energy by power to find a time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first electrical equation students meet is V = I R, which is usually rearranged by dividing, so division becomes the default operation.
misconceptions.correction: Check the words: power = potential difference x current. Both a larger pd and a larger current give a larger power, so the two must multiply.

misconceptions.question: A device has 12 V across it and 0.25 A through it. What is the power?
misconceptions.correct: P = V I = 3.0 W.
misconceptions.misconception: The power is 12 + 0.25 = 12.25 W.
misconceptions.whyItArises: When the operation is not recalled, adding the two given numbers feels safe because it uses both of them.
misconceptions.correction: Adding a pd in volts to a current in amperes adds unlike quantities. The equation multiplies them, and the product is in watts.

misconceptions.question: A current of 0.60 A flows through a 12 ohm resistor. What is the power?
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation looks like V = I R, and the small superscript 2 is easy to miss when reading quickly.
misconceptions.correction: Square the current first, then multiply by the resistance. Writing 0.60 x 0.60 x 12 out in full keeps the square visible.

misconceptions.question: The current in a fixed resistor is doubled. What happens to the power?
misconceptions.correct: P = I^2 R, so doubling the current makes the power four times greater.
misconceptions.misconception: Doubling the current doubles the power.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Direct proportion is the familiar pattern, and the square is treated as decoration rather than as part of the arithmetic.
misconceptions.correction: Substitute: (2I)^2 R = 4 I^2 R. Doubling a squared quantity multiplies the result by four.

misconceptions.question: What does a rating of 60 W tell you about a lamp?
misconceptions.correct: The watt is a unit of power, so the lamp transfers 60 J of energy every second.
misconceptions.misconception: The watt is a unit of energy, so the lamp uses 60 J in total.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Watts appear on appliances in contexts where students are asked about 'energy use', so the two ideas merge.
misconceptions.correction: One watt is one joule per second. A watt is a rate, so it always needs a time before it becomes an energy.

misconceptions.question: What does a current of 2 A tell you?
misconceptions.correct: Current is the rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes, A, and amp is acceptable for ampere.
misconceptions.misconception: The ampere measures the amount of electricity stored in a component, which the component then uses up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language talks about a battery 'holding electricity', so current is imagined as a quantity that sits in the circuit.
misconceptions.correction: Current is a flow, not a store, and it is not used up. Two amperes means two coulombs of charge passing each second.

misconceptions.question: A resistor is labelled 12 ohms. What does the ohm measure?
misconceptions.correct: The ohm is the unit of resistance, R.
misconceptions.misconception: The ohm is the unit of potential difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: V = I R links all three quantities, and students remember the equation rather than which unit belongs to which symbol.
misconceptions.correction: Match each symbol to its unit: R to ohms, V to volts, I to amperes, P to watts.

misconceptions.question: What does an electric heater do to energy?
misconceptions.correct: The heater transfers energy from the mains supply to the thermal store of the room. Energy is transferred, not created.
misconceptions.misconception: The heater creates or produces new energy from the electricity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Words such as 'generating' and 'producing power' are everyday usage, and appliances appear to make heat from nothing.
misconceptions.correction: Energy is only ever transferred between stores. Track where the energy came from as well as where it ends up.

misconceptions.question: A 2000 W kettle and a 100 W lamp are both switched on. Which transfers more energy?
misconceptions.correct: It depends on the time as well as the power: the lamp left on for an hour transfers more than the kettle used for two minutes.
misconceptions.misconception: The appliance switched on for the longer time is the more powerful one, because I confuse how long a device runs with how powerful it is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Power ratings are the only figures given on appliances, so they are treated as a complete answer on their own.
misconceptions.correction: Energy transferred = power x time. A comparison of energy needs both the power and the time for each appliance.

misconceptions.question: What is the main energy transfer in a food mixer?
misconceptions.correct: Energy is transferred electrically from the ac mains to the kinetic energy of the motor.
misconceptions.misconception: The main transfer is to the thermal store, because the mixer gets warm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All appliances warm up, and heating is the transfer students meet first, so it is offered for every device.
misconceptions.correction: Identify what the appliance is designed to do. A mixer is designed to turn a blade, so the useful transfer is to kinetic energy.

misconceptions.question: How does the supply to a cordless drill differ from the supply to a kettle?
misconceptions.correct: The drill is supplied by batteries, and the kettle is plugged into the ac mains.
misconceptions.misconception: I mix up which appliances run from batteries and which from the ac mains - e.g. thinking a mains kettle or mixer runs on batteries, or that a cordless drill runs from the mains.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The abbreviations ac and dc are easily swapped, and 'straight from the wall' suggests dc for the mains.
misconceptions.correction: Batteries give a direct current, always in one direction. The mains supply is an alternating current.

misconceptions.question: Is work done when a current flows through a lamp?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Work is done when charge flows in a circuit, and that work transfers energy to the lamp.
misconceptions.misconception: No work is done because nothing visibly moves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Work is first met as force x distance with a visible object moving, so an invisible charge flow does not look like work.
misconceptions.correction: Work is done whenever energy is transferred by a force. The source does work pushing charge around the circuit.

misconceptions.question: A 1500 W hairdryer runs for 4 minutes. How much energy is transferred?
misconceptions.correct: Convert first: 4 minutes = 240 s, so E = 1500 x 240 = 360 000 J.
misconceptions.misconception: E = 1500 x 4 = 6000 J, using the time in minutes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number in the question is used exactly as written, and the unit line for t is not checked.
misconceptions.correction: In E = P t the time must be in seconds. Convert minutes or hours to seconds before substituting.

misconceptions.question: A current of 5.0 A flows for 60 s through a 12 V motor. How much energy is transferred?
misconceptions.misconception: E = Q V = 5.0 x 12 = 60 J, using the current in place of the charge flow.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Current and charge flow are both about moving charge, and the current is the number given in the question.
misconceptions.correction: Charge flow is current x time. Work out Q first, then multiply by the potential difference.

misconceptions.question: A charge flow of 300 C passes through a pd of 12 V. How much energy is transferred?
misconceptions.misconception: E = Q / V = 25 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dividing is the habitual move for electrical equations, carried over from rearranging V = I R.
misconceptions.correction: Both a larger charge flow and a larger pd transfer more energy, so the quantities must be multiplied.

misconceptions.question: What unit is used for charge flow?
misconceptions.correct: Charge flow, Q, is measured in coulombs, C.
misconceptions.misconception: Charge flow is measured in amperes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge and current are both described loosely as 'electricity', and the ampere is the unit met first.
misconceptions.correction: The ampere is the unit of current, the rate of flow. The coulomb is the unit of the charge that has flowed.

misconceptions.question: What is the National Grid?
misconceptions.correct: It is a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
misconceptions.misconception: It is just the network of cables that carries electricity across the country.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The pylons and cables are the visible part of the system, while transformers are hidden inside substations.
misconceptions.correction: The transformers are part of the grid, and they are what make transmission over long distances efficient.

misconceptions.question: Which transformer is next to the transmission cables at the power station end?
misconceptions.correct: A step-up transformer increases the pd from the power station to the transmission cables.
misconceptions.misconception: A step-down transformer is used at the power station and a step-up transformer near homes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Step down' sounds like leaving the power station, and 'step up' sounds like arriving at the consumer.
misconceptions.correction: Follow the path: the pd is stepped up for transmission, then stepped down to a much lower value for domestic use.

misconceptions.question: Why is a high potential difference used in the transmission cables?
misconceptions.correct: A high pd means a low current for the same power, and P = I^2 R shows a low current wastes far less energy in the cables.
misconceptions.misconception: A high pd is used so that the energy travels along the cables faster.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Potential difference is imagined as a push that speeds the electricity up, so more pd sounds like a quicker delivery.
misconceptions.correction: The benefit is the reduced current, not a change of speed. Less current means less heating of the cables.

misconceptions.question: Do transformers increase the energy delivered to consumers?
misconceptions.correct: No. Transformers change the potential difference; they do not create energy or increase the power transferred.
misconceptions.misconception: A step-up transformer increases the power, so more energy reaches consumers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Step up' is heard as 'more of everything', and the increase in pd is assumed to increase the power too.
misconceptions.correction: When a transformer raises the pd it lowers the current in the same ratio, so the power transferred is not increased.

misconceptions.question: Two heaters transfer the same energy. Does that mean they have the same power?
misconceptions.correct: Not unless they were switched on for the same time. Power is the energy transferred per second.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy and power mean the same thing, so equal energy means equal power.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words are used interchangeably in everyday speech, as in 'the power used last month'.
misconceptions.correction: Power is a rate. Divide the energy transferred by the time in seconds to compare powers fairly.

misconceptions.question: A motor takes 5.0 A for 60 s from a 12 V supply. How much energy is transferred?
misconceptions.correct: Q = I t = 300 C, so E = Q V = 3600 J. The time is used once, to find the charge flow.
misconceptions.misconception: E = Q V is used with the time in seconds put in place of the charge flow: 12 x 60 = 720 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Q and t are both numbers taken from the same sentence, and both are needed, so the wrong one is substituted into E = Q V.
misconceptions.correction: Q is the charge that has flowed, in coulombs, found from current x time. Only then does it go into E = Q V.

misconceptions.question: How does raising the transmission pd reduce the energy wasted?
misconceptions.correct: It reduces the current, and the power wasted in the cables is I^2 R.
misconceptions.misconception: It reduces the resistance of the cables.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both changes would reduce the waste, and resistance is the quantity in the equation that students expect to be able to control.
misconceptions.correction: The cables have a fixed resistance. Only the current changes, and squaring it makes the saving large.

mcqs.stem: An electric kettle is plugged into the mains and switched on. Which statement best describes why the kettle is built as it is?

options.text: It is designed to create new energy from the mains supply that it uses.
options.rationale: Says energy is created; appliances only transfer energy between stores.

options.text: It is designed to store the electrical energy the mains delivers.
options.rationale: Treats the appliance as a store of electricity rather than a device that transfers energy.

options.text: It is designed to bring about a particular energy transfer.
options.rationale: Everyday electrical appliances are designed to bring about energy transfers, here to the thermal store of the water.

options.text: It is designed to use up the current flowing in from the mains.
options.rationale: Says current is used up, but the same current flows out of the kettle as flows in.

mcqs.stem: A 2000 W kettle is switched on for 2 minutes. A 100 W lamp is switched on for 1 hour. Which transfers more energy?

options.text: The kettle, because it has the higher power rating of the two appliances.
options.rationale: Uses power alone to compare energy, ignoring how long each is switched on.

options.text: The kettle, because its rating already gives the energy it transfers.
options.rationale: Reads the watt rating as an energy in joules.

options.text: They are equal, because both of them are supplied by the same mains.
options.rationale: Assumes a shared supply fixes the energy transferred.

options.text: The lamp, because energy transferred depends on the time as well as the power.
options.rationale: E = P t: 100 W for 3600 s is 360 000 J, while 2000 W for 120 s is only 240 000 J.

mcqs.stem: A hairdryer has a power of 1500 W. It is switched on for 4 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?

options.rationale: 1500 x 60, from using one minute instead of the four minutes given.
1500 x 4, from leaving the time in minutes instead of converting to seconds.
1500 / 4, from dividing the power by the time.

mcqs.stem: A food mixer is plugged into a wall socket and switched on. How is energy transferred while it is in use?

options.text: Electrically from the ac mains to the thermal store of the mixer motor.
options.rationale: Picks heating because the motor warms up; that is the wasteful transfer, not the designed one.

options.text: Electrically from batteries to the kinetic energy of the motor.
options.rationale: A mains-plugged mixer is not battery driven; batteries supply portable appliances.

options.text: Electrically from the ac mains to the kinetic energy of the motor.
options.rationale: A mixer is designed to turn a blade, so the useful transfer is to the kinetic energy of an electric motor.

options.text: From the mains supply to the chemical store of the mixer.
options.rationale: There is no chemical store being filled in a mains appliance.

mcqs.stem: A cordless drill and an electric kettle are both in use. Which statement about their supplies is correct?

options.text: The drill is supplied by batteries and the kettle by the ac mains.
options.rationale: Portable appliances are supplied by batteries; appliances plugged into sockets use the ac mains.

options.text: The drill is supplied by the ac mains and the kettle by its batteries.
options.rationale: Reverses the two supplies.

options.text: Both are supplied by the ac mains, as both contain a heating device.
options.rationale: Assumes every appliance heats and that every appliance is mains driven.

options.text: Both are supplied by batteries which are recharged after use.
options.rationale: A kettle is not battery driven; it draws its energy directly from the mains.

mcqs.stem: A lamp is connected to a cell and lights up. Which statement about work in this circuit is correct?

options.text: No work is done, because nothing in the circuit can be seen moving.
options.rationale: Requires visible motion for work; the moving charge is invisible but real.

options.text: Work is done, because the lamp uses up the current.
options.rationale: Thinks the current itself is consumed by the lamp (m09) rather than energy being transferred while charge is conserved.

options.text: Work is done, because charge is flowing through the lamp.
options.rationale: Work is done when charge flows in a circuit, and that work transfers energy to the lamp.

options.text: Work is done only while the lamp is warming up to temperature.
options.rationale: Limits the work to a start-up period, but charge keeps flowing throughout.

mcqs.stem: Which equation does the specification give for the energy transferred by electrical work in terms of power?

options.text: energy transferred = power x time, with the time measured in seconds.
options.rationale: This is the equation the specification gives for the energy transferred by electrical work, E = P t.

options.text: energy transferred = power / time, with the time given in seconds.
options.rationale: Divides instead of multiplying; that would give energy per second, not energy.

options.text: energy transferred = power x time, with time given in minutes.
options.rationale: Uses minutes; the specification gives time, t, in seconds, s.

options.text: energy transferred = power + time, with the time in seconds.
options.rationale: Adds a power to a time, which are unlike quantities.

mcqs.stem: A kettle has a power of 2000 W. It is switched on for 90 s. How much energy does it transfer?

options.rationale: 2000 + 90, from adding the power to the time.
2 x 90, from using the power as 2 kW without converting it to watts.
2000 / 90, from dividing the power by the time.
E = P t = 2000 x 90 = 180 000 J, with the power in watts and the time in seconds.

mcqs.stem: A lamp has a power of 60 W. It transfers 5400 J of energy. For how long was it switched on?

options.rationale: 5400 x 60, from multiplying when the equation has to be rearranged.
Rearranging E = P t gives t = E / P = 5400 / 60 = 90 s.
A place-value slip in the division: 5400 / 6 instead of 5400 / 60.
5400 + 60, from adding the two given values.

mcqs.stem: Which line gives the equation for energy transferred in terms of charge flow, with the correct units?

options.text: E = Q V, where Q is charge flow in amperes and V is the pd in volts.
options.rationale: Gives charge flow the unit of current.

options.text: E = Q V, where Q is charge flow in coulombs and V is pd in volts.
options.rationale: The specification gives energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference, E = Q V.

options.text: E = Q / V, where Q is charge flow in coulombs and V is the pd.
options.rationale: Divides charge by pd, so a larger pd would transfer less energy.

options.text: E = I V, where I is the current in A and V is pd in volts.
options.rationale: Uses current in place of charge flow; I V gives power, not energy.

mcqs.stem: A motor connected to a 12 V supply takes a current of 5.0 A for 60 s. How much energy is transferred?

options.rationale: 3600 x 60, from multiplying by the time a second time.
12 x 60, from using the time in seconds in place of the charge flow.
5.0 x 12, from using the current in place of the charge flow.

mcqs.stem: An electric motor transfers 5400 J of energy when the potential difference across it is 18 V. What charge flowed through it?

options.rationale: 5400 x 18, from multiplying when the equation has to be rearranged.
5400 + 18, from adding the two given values.
18 / 5400, from dividing the two values the wrong way round.
Rearranging E = Q V gives Q = E / V = 5400 / 18 = 300 C.

mcqs.stem: Which units does the specification give for energy transferred and for time in E = P t?

options.text: Energy in joules, J, and time in minutes, min.
options.rationale: Uses minutes for time; E = P t requires the time in seconds.

options.text: Energy in watts, W, and time in seconds, s.
options.rationale: Gives energy the unit of power.

options.text: Energy in joules, J, and time in seconds, s.
options.rationale: The specification gives energy transferred, E, in joules, J, and time, t, in seconds, s.

options.text: Energy is in joules, J, and time is in hours, h.
options.rationale: Uses hours for time, so the answer would be out by a factor of 3600.

mcqs.stem: Which units does the specification give for charge flow and for potential difference in E = Q V?

options.text: Charge flow in coulombs, C, and pd in volts, V.
options.rationale: The specification gives charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C, and potential difference, V, in volts, V.

options.text: Charge flow in amperes, A, and the pd in volts, V.
options.rationale: Gives charge flow the unit of current.

options.text: Charge flow in coulombs, C, and pd in ohms, Ω.
options.rationale: pd given the ohm (m10: the ohm is the unit of potential difference), while charge flow is correctly in coulombs.

options.text: Charge flow in joules, J, and the pd in volts, V.
options.rationale: Gives charge flow the unit of energy.

mcqs.stem: A circuit device is switched on. Which statement about the power of the device is correct?

options.text: Its power is the pd across it added to the current through it, giving watts.
options.rationale: Adds two unlike quantities; power = pd x current.

options.text: Its power is the total energy that it transfers, whatever the time taken.
options.rationale: Treats power as an energy rather than as a rate of energy transfer.

options.text: Its power is the pd across it times the current, and the energy given each second.
options.rationale: P = V I gives the power from the circuit quantities, and E = P t shows the same power as the energy transferred per second.

options.text: Its power is the current through it divided by the pd that is across it.
options.rationale: Divides the two quantities, so a larger pd would give a smaller power.

mcqs.stem: Heater X transfers 30 000 J in 60 s. Heater Y transfers 48 000 J in 120 s. Which heater has the greater power?

options.text: Heater Y, because it transfers more energy altogether than heater X does.
options.rationale: Compares total energy rather than energy transferred per second.

options.text: Heater Y, because it was switched on for the longer period of time.
options.rationale: Uses the operating time alone to judge power.

options.text: They have equal power, since both transfer their energy steadily.
options.rationale: Assumes a steady transfer means an equal rate of transfer.

options.text: Heater X, because it transfers 500 J each second and Y transfers 400 J.
options.rationale: P = E / t: X gives 30 000 / 60 = 500 W and Y gives 48 000 / 120 = 400 W.

mcqs.stem: A cook boils the same pan of water on a 2400 W hob and then on a 900 W hob. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The 2400 W hob transfers more total energy, because it has more power.
options.rationale: Equates higher power with more energy (m24), ignoring that boiling the same water needs about the same energy, just delivered faster.

options.text: The 2400 W hob raises the temperature of the water faster than the 900 W hob.
options.rationale: A higher power rating means the thermal store of the water is filled at a greater rate.

options.text: The 900 W hob raises the temperature of the water more quickly than the 2400 W hob.
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship between the power rating and the rate of transfer.

options.text: The 2400 W hob transfers just 2400 J in total before it is switched off.
options.rationale: Reads the power rating as a total energy in joules.

mcqs.stem: What is the National Grid?

options.text: A system of cables alone that links all of the power stations to consumers.
options.rationale: Leaves out the transformers, which are part of the grid.

options.text: A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of the National Grid.

options.text: A system of power stations that generates all of the energy consumers use.
options.rationale: Describes generation rather than the system that transfers the power.

options.text: A system of transformers that increases the energy that is sent to consumers.
options.rationale: Says transformers increase energy; they change the potential difference.

mcqs.stem: Electrical power is transferred from a power station to homes. In which order are transformers used along the way?

options.text: Step-down transformers first, then step-up transformers near the consumers.
options.rationale: Reverses the order of the two transformers along the grid.

options.text: Step-up transformers at both ends, to keep the pd high all the way.
options.rationale: Would deliver mains electricity at a dangerously high potential difference.

options.text: Step-up transformers first, then step-down transformers near consumers.
options.rationale: Step-up transformers raise the pd for the transmission cables; step-down transformers lower it to a much lower value for domestic use.

options.text: No transformers are needed; the cables carry it straight to homes.
options.rationale: Sees the grid as just a network of cables (m20), so assumes no transformers are involved.

mcqs.stem: Why is the National Grid an efficient way to transfer energy from power stations to consumers?

options.text: A high pd gives a low current, so less energy is wasted heating the cables.
options.rationale: For a given power, raising the pd lowers the current, and the power wasted is I^2 R.

options.text: A high pd makes the energy travel along the transmission cables much faster.
options.rationale: Treats pd as controlling a speed; the benefit is the reduced current.

options.text: A high pd lowers the resistance of the long cables used in the National Grid.
options.rationale: The resistance of the cables is fixed; only the current changes.

options.text: A high pd increases the power that the power station is able to supply.
options.rationale: Transformers do not increase the power transferred.

mcqs.stem: A transmission cable of resistance 5.0 ohms carries a current of 1000 A. What power is wasted in heating the cable?

options.rationale: 2 x 1000 x 5.0, from doubling the current instead of squaring it.
1000 x 5.0, from missing the square on the current.
1000 / 5.0, from dividing the current by the resistance.
P = I^2 R = 1000^2 x 5.0 = 5 000 000 W wasted in heating the cable.
